title: Re-estimating & schedule optimisation
blurb: Explain why and when to re-estimate, the benefits it brings, and how crashing, fast-tracking and re-sequencing optimise a schedule.
question: A rail operator's ticket-gate upgrade has just passed its design gate. The new estimates show installation will run three weeks past the date promised to the public. The sponsor asks whether the team should have stuck with the original estimate, and how the lost time could be won back. What should the project manager say?

teach.h: Estimates are revisited, not set in stone
teach.body: Re-estimating means revisiting time, cost and resource estimates throughout the life cycle as better information becomes available. Early figures rest on assumptions; later ones can use detailed designs, quotes and actual performance. Plain English: update your forecast when you know more. A changed estimate is not a failure. It is the project telling you the truth early enough to act on it.

teach.caption: Widths are illustrative. A narrowing range reflects reduced uncertainty from better information, not a team suddenly working harder.

teach.h: Why re-estimate, and what you gain
teach.caption: Typical moments: decision gates, approved change requests, the end of each time box, and whenever a key assumption changes.

teach.text: Re-estimating is NOT the same as re-baselining. A new estimate updates the forecast; the baseline only changes through change control with the right approval. Equally, sticking to an out-of-date estimate does not protect the date: it only hides the problem until it is too late to fix.

teach.body: Schedule optimisation means improving the schedule, usually to shorten it or make it achievable, without changing the project's objectives. The main techniques are crashing (adding resources to critical activities, at extra cost), fast-tracking (overlapping activities normally done in sequence, at extra risk), re-sequencing (changing the order of work where the logic allows) and resource smoothing or levelling. Only changes to the critical path can bring the end date forward.

rows.label: What you do
values: Change the order where logic allows

teach.caption: Resource smoothing and levelling are also optimisation techniques: see the resource lessons in this topic.
Illustrative. Overlapping manufacture with the end of design saves a week, but if the design changes late, parts already made may need rework.
Illustrative. A second crew on the critical installation brings go-live forward. Adding staff to the signage would cost more and save nothing, because it is not critical.

rows.label: Re-estimate when
values: At gates, on changes, as actuals arrive
Every time box, using delivery so far

rows.label: What stays fixed
values: Time box dates and team capacity

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Reason: information improves through the life cycle (the estimating funnel), and changes, risks and actual performance alter the picture.
Benefits: more accurate forecasts, realistic baselines, early warning of problems and better-informed decisions.
Optimisation: name crashing (resources, cost), fast-tracking (overlap, risk) and re-sequencing (order, where logic allows).
Stress that only shortening the critical path brings the end date forward.
Note that baseline changes go through change control, and iterative projects flex scope rather than dates.
Re-estimate throughout the life cycle as information improves, at gates and after changes.
Benefits: accurate forecasts, realistic baselines, early warning, better decisions.
Crashing: add resources to critical activities, at a cost.
Fast-tracking: overlap activities normally in sequence, at extra risk of rework.
Re-sequencing: change the order where logic allows; baseline changes need change control.

summary: You can now explain why estimates are revisited throughout the life cycle and the benefits re-estimating brings. You can also differentiate crashing, fast-tracking and re-sequencing, say what each costs, and explain why only changes to the critical path can bring the end date forward.

A.q: What is the main reason estimates are revisited as a project moves through its life cycle?
options: To show the sponsor the team is busy
Better information reduces uncertainty
To replace the need for change control
Earlier estimates are always discarded
A.why: As designs, quotes and actual progress become available, uncertainty falls. Re-estimating uses that better information to produce more reliable forecasts.

whyNot.0: Re-estimating is about accuracy, not demonstrating activity.
whyNot.2: Change control is still needed to alter the baseline.
whyNot.3: Earlier estimates are refined, and their assumptions checked, rather than simply thrown away.

A.q: Which of the following is a benefit of re-estimating throughout a project?
options: It guarantees the original date is met
It removes the need for any contingency
It gives early warning of likely overruns
It stops stakeholders from asking for changes
A.why: Updated estimates reveal problems while there is still time to act, giving early warning and better-informed decisions.

whyNot.0: Re-estimating can show the original date is at risk; it cannot guarantee it.
whyNot.1: Uncertainty remains, so contingency is still needed.
whyNot.3: Re-estimating does not prevent change requests.

A.q: A project manager adds a second team to a critical activity to finish it sooner, accepting a higher cost. Which technique is this?
options: Crashing
Fast-tracking
Re-sequencing
Resource levelling
A.why: Crashing adds resources to critical activities to shorten their duration, at extra cost.

whyNot.1: Fast-tracking overlaps activities rather than adding resources.
whyNot.2: Re-sequencing changes the order of activities, not the resources on them.
whyNot.3: Levelling delays activities to fit resource limits and may lengthen the project.

B.q: A web agency starts building pages before the design has been fully signed off, so the two activities overlap. What is the main risk of this approach?
options: Resource costs rise for each extra person
The critical path becomes longer than before
Late design changes may force rework
Float on every activity is reduced to zero
B.why: This is fast-tracking. Work starts on assumptions about the design, so if the design changes late, completed build work may have to be redone.

whyNot.0: Rising cost for extra people is the trade-off of crashing.
whyNot.1: Fast-tracking is intended to shorten the critical path, not lengthen it.
whyNot.3: Overlapping two activities does not remove float from every activity.

B.q: A specialist surveyor is overloaded because three of her tasks fall in the same fortnight. The project manager changes the order of work so she does them one after another where the logic allows. Which technique is this?
options: Re-sequencing
Crashing
Fast-tracking
Analytical estimating
B.why: Changing the order of activities, within the logic, to ease a bottleneck is re-sequencing.

whyNot.1: Crashing would add resources, such as a second surveyor.
whyNot.2: Fast-tracking overlaps activities, which would make the overload worse.
whyNot.3: Analytical estimating is a way of producing estimates, not of reordering work.

B.q: To pull the end date forward, a project manager adds staff to an activity with three weeks of float. What is the most likely result?
options: Costs rise but the end date does not move
The end date moves forward by three weeks
The activity becomes part of the critical path
Float on the critical path increases instead
B.why: The activity is not on the critical path, so finishing it sooner does not shorten the project. The extra staff simply add cost.

whyNot.1: Only shortening critical activities can bring the end date forward.
whyNot.2: Finishing a non-critical activity sooner gives it more float, not less.
whyNot.3: Critical activities have zero float; changing a non-critical one does not alter that.

C.q: At a decision gate, a re-estimate shows the project will finish beyond the sponsor's agreed time tolerance. What should the project manager do?
options: Quietly update the baseline to the new date
Keep reporting the old date until delivery
Raise it and propose options for a decision
Cut testing so the original date is met
C.why: A forecast beyond tolerance must be escalated. The project manager presents options (such as crashing, fast-tracking or a change to scope or date) so the sponsor can decide, and any baseline change goes through change control.

whyNot.0: Changing the baseline without approval bypasses change control and governance.
whyNot.1: Hiding the forecast removes the early warning that makes re-estimating valuable.
whyNot.3: Cutting testing trades a visible delay for hidden quality risk without any approval.

C.q: Two weeks before the end of a time box, an iterative team realises not all the planned items will be finished. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Extend the time box until everything is done
Crash the time box by working every weekend
Release the unfinished items untested on time
Reprioritise and defer lower-priority items
C.why: In an iterative life cycle the time box is fixed and scope flexes. The team re-estimates what can be finished and defers lower-priority items to a later time box.

whyNot.0: Extending the time box breaks the fixed-time principle of iterative working.
whyNot.1: Sustained overtime is not the iterative response and damages the team's capacity.
whyNot.2: Releasing untested items puts quality at risk.

C.q: Which TWO are benefits of re-estimating? 1. Realistic baselines 2. A guarantee of no change requests 3. Better-informed decisions 4. No need for contingency
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
C.why: Re-estimating supports realistic baselines (1) and better-informed decisions (3), as well as more accurate forecasts and early warning.

whyNot.1: Neither is a benefit: change requests still happen and contingency is still needed.
whyNot.2: Uncertainty remains, so contingency is still needed (4).

reteach.title: Think of organising a music festival
reteach.question: Months out, you guess the stage build will take a week. Then the stage designs arrive, the crew quotes come in, and set-up starts. What do you do with your guess, and how can you claw back time if it slips?

blocks.h: Update the guess, then pull the levers
blocks.body: Your first guess was made with almost nothing to go on, so you update it when the designs and quotes arrive: that is re-estimating. If the build is now too long, you have levers. Hire a second crew for the main stage (crashing: costs more). Start rigging lights before the stage roof is fully finished (fast-tracking: risk of redoing work). Build the bars before the stage so the crane is free when the stage needs it (re-sequencing).

head: Lever
Festival example
Price you pay
rows: Second crew on the main stage
Rig lights before the roof is done

blocks.text: Hiring a second crew for the merchandise tent won't open the gates any sooner: it isn't on the critical path.

explain.body: Re-estimate when information improves (designs, quotes, actuals), when changes are approved, when risks occur or close, when assumptions prove wrong, and at decision gates or the end of each time box.

test.q: A supplier tells a project that a key component's lead time is twelve weeks, not the six weeks assumed. What should the project manager do first?
options: Keep the six-week figure to avoid concern
Wait until the component actually arrives
Ask the supplier to absorb the difference
Re-estimate the affected activities now
test.why: A key assumption has proved wrong, which is a clear trigger to re-estimate the affected activities and check the impact on the critical path.

whyNot.0: Holding on to a known-wrong assumption hides the problem.
whyNot.1: Waiting removes the chance to act early.
whyNot.2: Negotiation may help later, but the forecast must first reflect reality.

explain.body: As information improves, the range around an estimate narrows. That reflects reduced uncertainty, not a change in effort. Explaining this helps stakeholders understand why early figures were ranges.

test.q: A sponsor notices successive estimates have narrowed and says the team must be working harder. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The team is working more hours than planned
Uncertainty has fallen as information improved
The scope has been reduced without approval
The baseline has been quietly re-set lower
test.why: A narrowing range is the estimating funnel at work: more information means less uncertainty, so the range tightens.

whyNot.0: The width of an estimate's range reflects uncertainty, not effort.
whyNot.2: Unapproved scope reduction would be a control failure, not the normal reason ranges narrow.
whyNot.3: Estimates narrowing is not a baseline change; that needs change control.

explain.body: Crashing adds resources to critical activities: it mainly costs money. Fast-tracking overlaps activities normally done in sequence: it mainly adds risk, because later work starts on incomplete information.

test.q: Which schedule optimisation technique mainly increases cost rather than the risk of rework?
options: Fast-tracking
Crashing
Re-sequencing
Three-point estimating
test.why: Crashing buys time with extra resources, so its main trade-off is cost.

whyNot.0: Fast-tracking's main trade-off is the risk of rework from overlapping activities.
whyNot.2: Re-sequencing changes the order of work; it does not mainly add cost.
whyNot.3: Three-point estimating produces ranges; it is not an optimisation technique.

explain.body: Pick the lever that fits the constraint. Budget available and little appetite for rework risk: crashing. Fixed budget and some risk accepted: fast-tracking. A bottleneck on one resource: re-sequencing. Whatever you choose, apply it to the critical path.

test.q: A project must finish earlier, its budget is fixed, and two critical activities could safely partly overlap. Which technique is most suitable?
options: Crashing
Resource levelling
Fast-tracking
Analogous estimating
test.why: With no extra budget for resources, overlapping the critical activities (fast-tracking) is the way to save time, accepting some extra risk.

whyNot.0: Crashing needs extra resources, which a fixed budget rules out.
whyNot.1: Levelling fits work to resource limits and may extend the end date.
whyNot.3: Analogous estimating produces estimates; it does not shorten the schedule.
